facts.claim: Amy Edmondson's research made psychological safety a team-level learning condition.
facts.mechanism: Because teams learn from errors only when people can raise concerns without disproportionate interpersonal penalty.
facts.commonError: Treating psychological safety as comfort or niceness.
facts.whyWrong: The construct is about candor and learning behavior, not avoiding standards.

facts.claim: Hospital teams are a concrete setting for psychological safety because error reporting affects learning.
facts.mechanism: Because unspoken mistakes keep the system from detecting and correcting weak processes.
facts.commonError: Assuming silence means few errors occurred.
facts.whyWrong: Silence can mean people are afraid to report or discuss what went wrong.

facts.claim: Google Project Aristotle studied 180 teams while looking for drivers of team effectiveness.
facts.mechanism: Because a multi-team analysis shows that contribution patterns are shaped by group conditions.
facts.commonError: Explaining team performance only by individual resumes.
facts.whyWrong: Team norms can change whether capable individuals speak and learn.

facts.claim: Psychological safety supports candor but does not remove performance standards.
facts.mechanism: Because people need enough safety to speak and enough challenge to improve the work.
facts.commonError: Believing safety means lowering the bar.
facts.whyWrong: Safety without standards becomes comfort; standards without safety become fear.

facts.claim: Pixar's Braintrust centers candid feedback on improving unfinished creative work.
facts.mechanism: Because feedback is safer and more useful when it is framed around the work product rather than personal status.
facts.commonError: Using candor as a license for harsh personal judgment.
facts.whyWrong: The useful target is the problem in the work, not the dignity of the maker.

facts.claim: A liberating room reduces leader-centered threat.
facts.mechanism: Because people contribute more when attention is on the problem instead of protecting themselves from the leader.
facts.commonError: Thinking the leader must dominate the room to create seriousness.
facts.whyWrong: Domination can produce compliance while reducing usable intelligence.

facts.claim: Fear can imitate discipline while hiding the information a team most needs.
facts.mechanism: Because intimidated people avoid sharing weak signals, mistakes, and dissent, the leader receives a cleaner but less accurate picture.
facts.whyWrong: Quiet can indicate suppression rather than agreement.

facts.claim: Liberation requires explicit permission for dissent and unfinished thinking.
facts.mechanism: Because many employees will not risk partial ideas unless the leader makes exploration legitimate.
facts.commonError: Waiting for people to volunteer risky thoughts without changing the climate.
facts.whyWrong: The environment tells people whether contribution is worth the risk.

facts.claim: High standards are more credible when people can question the path to meeting them.
facts.mechanism: Because challenge improves when contributors can test assumptions and surface obstacles before failure becomes expensive.
facts.commonError: Protecting standards by shutting down questions.
facts.whyWrong: Questions can strengthen execution by exposing weak assumptions early.

allowedAnchors.label: liberating climate
allowedAnchors.text: A liberating climate gives people room to contribute honestly while making clear that the standard remains high. Safety and stretch work together: people are not protected from effort, but they are protected from needless intimidation. A reader who gets the distinction stops choosing between comfort and accountability. The better target is a room where candor is safe and weak thinking is still challenged.
